analysis.one_liner: Ends a range of corporate subsidies and tax breaks, and makes mining companies pay royalties and clean up public lands.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to seven House committees, was never taken up by any of them, and died without a vote when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal several federal subsidies that go mainly to corporations: tax breaks for overseas export income and for alcohol fuels, farm export promotion and tobacco price supports, the Advanced Technology Program, TVA appropriations, federal funding of logging roads in national forests, and funds for the International Monetary Fund. It would also replace the 1872 mining law's rules for hardrock mining on public lands with a modern system: companies would pay an 8% royalty on minerals taken from public land, pay claim fees, get permits, post financial assurance, and reclaim the land when done. Money raised would go to a fund to clean up abandoned mines and reduce the deficit.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who currently fund the subsidies and get no financial return for minerals taken from public lands; people living near abandoned mines, who would benefit from a new reclamation fund; and users of public lands affected by unregulated mining and federally funded logging roads.

how_it_helps.text: The bill states that the 1872 mining law transfers mineral-bearing public land to private hands below fair market value and provides no financial return to the American people; the bill would impose an 8% royalty on minerals and fees on mining claims [S3].

It would repeal tax exclusions for foreign sales corporations, incentives for alcohol fuels, the Export Enhancement Program, the Market Promotion Program, tobacco price supports, the Advanced Technology Program, TVA appropriations, and federal funding of logging roads [S2][S3].
All fees and royalties collected from mining would go into a new Abandoned Locatable Minerals Mine Reclamation Fund to clean up mined lands that pose threats to public health and safety [S2][S3].

Mining on federal land would require permits with reclamation plans, financial assurance, inspections, and citizen suits to enforce compliance; revenues from the changes would be dedicated to deficit reduction [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The industries receiving the subsidies: hardrock mining companies, ethanol and alcohol-fuel producers, exporters using foreign sales corporations, farm export programs and tobacco growers, timber operators using national forest roads, and TVA's non-power programs. Some costs, such as the end of ethanol fuel tax credits, could slightly raise fuel prices for consumers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Mining, timber, ethanol, tobacco, agribusiness interests

drawbacks.text: Repealing the alcohol-fuel incentives would tax fuel alcohol the same as other motor fuels and even imposed a one-time floor stock tax of 18.4 cents per gallon on fuel alcohol held on January 1, 1998, a cost that could be passed to consumers [S3].

Ending tobacco price supports and quotas and agribusiness export subsidies would cut income in rural communities dependent on those programs, even though taxpayers would stop paying for them [S2][S3].

The bill's own findings acknowledge the tension that royalties and fees must not be set so high as to discourage a capital-intensive domestic mining industry that provides thousands of jobs; critics of mining reform have long argued new costs could shift production overseas [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill attacked real, continuing transfers of public money and public resources to private interests, and its mining title addressed documented harms: unreclaimed mine sites that the bill text says threaten public health, safety, and the environment. The main costs are concentrated in a handful of industries and regions, and the ethanol repeal would have modestly raised fuel costs. On balance the benefits to taxpayers and public lands outweigh the sectoral costs, though the bill was broad and unpolished, spanning seven committee jurisdictions.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to seven House committees, scattered among a dozen subcommittees, none of which ever reported it, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter Visclosky introduced the Corporate Responsibility Act of 1997 on April 15, 1997 [S1][S5].
The bill was referred to seven committees: Ways and Means, Resources, Agriculture, Science, Banking and Financial Services, Budget, and Transportation and Infrastructure [S1][S5].

In the following two weeks, provisions were sent to a dozen subcommittees, including Energy and Mineral Resources, Forests and Forest Health, Technology, Domestic and International Monetary Policy, Water Resources and Environment, and several Agriculture subcommittees; the Interior Department was asked for its comments [S5].
No committee ever reported the bill, no hearing or markup is recorded in its action history, and it received no floor vote before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The subsidized industries kept the status quo: mining companies continued taking public-land minerals without paying a royalty, and exporters, ethanol producers, tobacco growers, timber operators, and TVA kept their federal support.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Mining, timber, ethanol, and tobacco interests

for.name: Rep. Peter J. Visclosky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Corporate Responsibility Act of 1997 to cut corporate subsidies and reform hardrock mining on public lands.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out of committee; its tax provisions (foreign sales corporation exclusions, alcohol fuel incentives) died there.

against.name: House Resources Committee
against.role: Committee of referral with jurisdiction over the mining title
against.what_they_did: Sent the mining provisions to the Energy and Mineral Resources and Forests and Forest Health subcommittees and never acted further.

against.name: Hardrock mining industry
against.role: Principal beneficiary of the Mining Law of 1872
against.what_they_did: The bill's findings describe an industry that pays no royalty and buys public land below fair value; industry groups actively opposed mining-law reform efforts during this Congress, and no mining-committee action followed.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsor Visclosky was a Democrat and 3 of his 5 cosponsors were Republicans, but no committee or floor vote was ever recorded, so there is no roll-call record of how the parties stood.

industries.note: The bill would end their ability to extract gold, silver, and other hardrock minerals from public land without paying a royalty, requiring an 8% net smelter return royalty, claim fees, permits, reclamation bonds, and cleanup liability. The bill's own findings state the 1872 law transfers mineral-bearing public land to private ownership below fair market value with no return to the public.

The bill repeals the alcohol-fuel tax incentives and excise-tax exemptions that subsidize ethanol blended into motor fuel; ending the subsidy would raise the cost of producing and selling ethanol blends, with some pass-through to fuel prices.

Repeal of the Export Enhancement Program and Market Promotion Program would end federal export promotion payments to agribusiness, and elimination of tobacco price supports and quotas would end a federal program that propped up tobacco prices. Taxpayers would save; individual growers and exporters would lose income.

The bill would eliminate purchaser road credits — credits loggers received for building national forest roads — and bar federal funding of roads used principally for logging, requiring the Forest Service to recover road costs from logging users.
Repealing the foreign sales corporation exclusion would subject billions in export income to U.S. tax; large multinationals used FSCs to reduce taxes on export income.

industries.industry: High-tech firms receiving Advanced Technology Program grants
industries.note: The bill abolishes the Advanced Technology Program, which provided federal cost-sharing grants to companies for technology development, and rescinds unobligated funds.
The bill bars any U.S. officer or employee from providing federal funds to the IMF under its New Arrangements to Borrow facility.
